\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{انتقد} (intaqada)}{انتقد (intaqada)}]{\ar{انتقد} (intaqada) — to criticize}

\label{lesson:AR-C370-intaqada}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for to hesitate, then the Arabic for an alternative.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{انتقد}}
\textbf{\ar{انتقد}} — \emph{intaqada} — \textquotedblleft{}to criticize\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{انتقد} \ar{المدرب} \ar{أداء} \ar{اللاعبين}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{intaqada al-mudarrib adāʾ al-lāʿibīn.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
The coach criticized the players' performance.
\end{quote}

Present: \ar{ينتقد}, \emph{yantaqid}.

The noun \ar{انتقاد}, \emph{intiqād}, criticism.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{انتقد}} (\emph{intaqada}) is built on the native Arabic root \emph{n-q-d}, \textquotedblleft{}to sort good coins from bad\textquotedblright{} (Lane). It is Form VIII, to pick out the good from the bad: to judge, to criticize.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for giving reasons and opinions.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{intaqada}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{intaqada}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{intaqada al-mudarrib adāʾ al-lāʿibīn.} — The coach criticized the players' performance.
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Arabic for to hesitate, then the Arabic for an alternative, then say \emph{intaqada} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ar{انتقد} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To criticize\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{عارض} (ʿāraḍa)}{عارض (ʿāraḍa)}]{\ar{عارض} (ʿāraḍa) — to oppose}

\label{lesson:AR-C370-aarada}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for an alternative, then the Arabic for to criticize.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{عارض}}
\textbf{\ar{عارض}} — \emph{ʿāraḍa} — \textquotedblleft{}to oppose\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{عارض} \ar{بعض} \ar{السكان} \ar{المشروع} \ar{الجديد}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{ʿāraḍa baʿḍ as-sukkān al-mashrūʿ al-jadīd.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
Some residents opposed the new project.
\end{quote}

Present: \ar{يعارض}, \emph{yuʿāriḍ}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{عارض}} (\emph{ʿāraḍa}) is built on the native Arabic root \emph{ʿ-r-ḍ}, \textquotedblleft{}to be broad; to lie across\textquotedblright{} (Lane). It is Form III, to set oneself across from: to oppose.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for giving reasons and opinions.
\end{grammarlens}

\end{itemize}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{برر} (barrara)}{برر (barrara)}]{\ar{برر} (barrara) — to justify}

\label{lesson:AR-C370-barrara}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for to criticize, then the Arabic for to oppose.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{برر}}
\textbf{\ar{برر}} — \emph{barrara} — \textquotedblleft{}to justify\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{برر} \ar{الموظف} \ar{تأخره} \ar{بالمطر}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{barrara al-muwaẓẓaf taʾakhkhurahu bi-l-maṭar.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
The employee gave the rain as the reason for his lateness.
\end{quote}

Present: \ar{يبرر}, \emph{yubarrir}.

The noun \ar{تبرير}, \emph{tabrīr}, a justification.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{برر}} (\emph{barrara}) is built on the native Arabic root \emph{b-r-r}, \textquotedblleft{}to be true, to be good\textquotedblright{} (Lane). It is Form II, to show to be right: to justify.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for giving reasons and opinions.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{بالغ} (bālagha)}{بالغ (bālagha)}]{\ar{بالغ} (bālagha) — to exaggerate}

\label{lesson:AR-C370-balagha}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for to oppose, then the Arabic for to justify.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{بالغ}}
\textbf{\ar{بالغ}} — \emph{bālagha} — \textquotedblleft{}to exaggerate\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{بالغ} \ar{صديقي} \ar{في} \ar{وصف} \ar{الفندق}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{bālagha ṣadīqī fī waṣf al-funduq.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
My friend exaggerated in describing the hotel.
\end{quote}

Present: \ar{يبالغ}, \emph{yubāligh}.

It takes \ar{في}: \ar{بالغ} \ar{في} ….

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{بالغ}} (\emph{bālagha}) is built on the native Arabic root \emph{b-l-gh}, \textquotedblleft{}to reach\textquotedblright{} (Lane). It is Form III, to strive to reach the utmost: to overdo, to exaggerate.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for giving reasons and opinions.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{عمم} (ʿammama)}{عمم (ʿammama)}]{\ar{عمم} (ʿammama) — to generalize}

\label{lesson:AR-C370-ammama}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for to justify, then the Arabic for to exaggerate.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{عمم}}
\textbf{\ar{عمم}} — \emph{ʿammama} — \textquotedblleft{}to generalize\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{لا} \ar{يجوز} \ar{أن} \ar{نعمم} \ar{من} \ar{مثال} \ar{واحد}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{lā yajūzu an nuʿammima min mithāl wāḥid.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
We should not generalize from one example.
\end{quote}

Present: \ar{يعمم}, \emph{yuʿammim}.

The noun \ar{تعميم}, \emph{taʿmīm}, a generalization.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{عمم}} (\emph{ʿammama}) is built on the native Arabic root \emph{ʿ-m-m}, \textquotedblleft{}to be general, to include all\textquotedblright{} (Lane). It is Form II, to make general: to generalize.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for giving reasons and opinions.
\end{grammarlens}
